source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 2026): contract Design Engineer, May–Oct 2026, only designer; founders + a team of 6+ (roles not stated); built the prompt bar, workspace layout, deploy and web screens in React/TypeScript, mostly with Claude Code and Cursor; the board was his idea, people found it slightly confusing (more used to chatting with an agent), it was too much to build, and the founders/team chose chat-first; the board may return; dual sidebar consolidated after people found two collapsible panes a bit confusing; 8 picker frames are 8 iterations, changed after tester feedback and own critique (unclear what Apply did, unclear what was selected); after the changes shipped people stopped hitting those problems; colour restraint was his call; workspace, prompt bar, deploy and web app are live; the work helped grow ARR (user count private); audience is technical and non-technical people. Takeaways he chose: 'states, not screens' and 'right idea, wrong time'. Depth round (Nov 2026): modes moved out of a dropdown after PostHog showed Plan/Ask were rarely used and support asked for an ask-only mode that already existed; only the active mode is labelled to stay narrow, say what will happen and reduce noise; agent work is folded for non-technical users and readability, expanded logs give each step an icon and code/commands their own containers; remote/local can't change after a session starts and the model rarely changes, so both sit under the bar only at the start; new sessions get a taller bar to feel balanced and important; the queue exists because runs take minutes, people wanted to line up the next change, and it keeps them in control. Title: Winston asked for 'Newly Desktop App' (Nov 2026); the slug stays as is. Copy round (Nov 2026): never say 'assumed' or that numbers are missing; just leave it out. Each case ends with a short Summary that doesn't mention what's missing or assumed. Layout (Nov 2026): per Winston's V3 design, the How might we statement is the heading of the first content section, titled 'Problem Statement'; the summary field is a short line on what he did. Round 2 (Nov 17 2026): the board-with-prompt-bar image is shown without its wallpaper; the board caption is removed. Start screen (335:7662 no project, 284:37196 in a project): the sidebar differs in and out of a project; the taller prompt bar is for attention; there is space for a card stack to resume projects or promote actions like downloading the mobile app. Menus had to give clear information without much text: one-line location trade-offs, the effort slider, and a small LINK button that prompts people to link their own agents. He used Claude Design to prototype the chat interactions and layouts, because he could simulate typing and chatting with the agent while iterating (canvas: Chat screen design experiments). A lot of the onboarding was designed and then prototyped in Claude Design (canvas: Newly App Onboarding Flow); the clips are recorded from that prototype.

fields.title: Newly Desktop App
fields.description: One prompt bar, a live iPhone preview and a path to the App Store.
fields.intro: Newly is an AI agent that turns a conversation into a real iOS, Android or web app. As a contract design engineer and the only designer, I designed the desktop and web workspace and built parts of it in React and TypeScript.
fields.summary: I designed the workspace where people build apps with Newly’s agent, from the prompt bar to deploying to the App Store.
fields.overview: Newly is for technical and non-technical people alike. I worked with the founders and a team of six-plus, and changed course when feedback showed something wasn’t working.
fields.impact: Shipped on desktop and web, and helped grow Newly’s revenue.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we let anyone build and ship a real app with an AI agent, without losing track of what it’s doing?
content: One text box drives local and cloud sessions, a simulator, git branches, model choices and releases to TestFlight and the App Store.

bullets: **Who:** technical and non-technical people.
**Where:** a desktop app and the web.
**Constraint:** more ideas than time to build them.

sections.title: Board vs. chat
sections.heading: Board or chat
content: I explored a few ways of working with the agent.

board.label: Ways to work with the agent

notes.text: A board where the agent proposes features you approve, build and deploy
A prompt bar above the board
Chat-first: just chat with the agent

content: My first direction treated your app like a roadmap. The agent proposed features as cards and explained its reasoning. You approved, built and deployed each one from a board.

content.alt: Early Newly workspace with a board of proposed features, the agent’s reasoning panel for one feature, and a live iPhone preview
content.caption: The board, with the agent’s reasoning open.

content: Another version put a prompt bar above the board.

gallery.alt: Newly home as a three-column board of proposed features
Newly home with a Welcome Back prompt bar above the feature board
The chat-first Newly workspace with sessions, conversation and a running iPhone simulator

content.caption: Board, then board with a prompt bar, then the chat-first direction that shipped.

bullets: **People found the board slightly confusing.** They were more used to just chatting with an agent.
**It was too much to build** in the time we had.
**The founders and team chose chat-first,** and I designed the workspace around it.

content: The board is still in the file, and we might bring it back.

sections.title: Sidebar
sections.heading: One sidebar instead of two
content: The workspace is made of panes you can open and collapse: sessions, chat and the app preview. I built this layout in code.

At first, app navigation and the session list were separate panes. Both could collapse, and the session list also acted like navigation. People found that a bit confusing, so we merged them into one sidebar.

gallery.alt: Earlier Newly layout with an app navigation pane (Create, Deploy, Analytics, Settings) next to a separate Sessions pane
gallery.label: Before

gallery.alt: Final Newly layout with one sidebar: New Session, Search, Deploy and Configure above pinned sessions and the session list, next to the chat and app preview
gallery.label: After

content.caption: Two collapsible panes, then one sidebar.

sections.title: Onboarding
sections.heading: From sign-up to the first prompt
content: I designed the onboarding, then prototyped a lot of it in Claude Design, micro-interactions and animations included.

content.caption: The welcome screen cycles through things you could make, then sign-up.

content: Next come two quick questions: what you want to build, and how much of this you’ve done before. Every option has a one-line hint, like “Explain things as we go” or “Give me the controls”, and both questions can be skipped. A three-card tour follows: say it once in plain English, change anything by asking, ship it to the App Store.

content.caption: What you’re building, how much you’ve done before, and the tour.

content: Local development needs Xcode and an iPhone simulator. Newly runs both setups for you, one step at a time, and shows each step as it runs. **Set this up later** skips it.

content.caption: Xcode and the simulator set up, then the workspace opens.

sections.title: Start screen
sections.heading: One start screen, in and out of a project
content: Every new chat starts on the same screen, with or without a project open. What changes is the sidebar:

bullets: **No project open:** Home, Open Existing Project and Docs, then your projects and recent ones.
**Inside a project:** the project, New Session, Search, Deploy and Configure, then pinned sessions and the session list.

content: The prompt bar is taller here than in a chat, so starting one gets your attention and the screen feels balanced.
Below it there’s room for a stack of cards: a way back into a recent project, or an action worth promoting, like getting the mobile app.

gallery.label: No project
gallery.alt: Newly with no project open: a sidebar with Home, Open Existing Project, Docs, projects and recents, a tall prompt bar under Let’s make something new, and a Summer Project card to pick up where you left off

gallery.label: In a project
gallery.alt: Newly inside the Travel App project: a sidebar with New Session, Search, Deploy, Configure, pinned sessions and sessions, a tall prompt bar under Hey Winston! Ready to build?, and a card to try the Newly mobile app

content.caption: “Pick up where you left off” outside a project, “Try the Newly Mobile App” inside one.

sections.title: Prompt bar
sections.heading: One prompt bar, three layouts
content: I built the prompt bar in React and TypeScript, mostly with Claude Code and Cursor. It appears across the workspace and changes with the space it has and what the agent is doing.

In the old product, Build, Plan and Ask sat in a dropdown. PostHog showed people rarely used Plan or Ask, and some support requests asked for a mode that only answers questions without editing anything. That mode already existed. People just couldn’t find it.
So the modes moved into the bar as a segmented control, and only the active one shows its label:

bullets: **It stays narrow** enough for every width.
**It always says what will happen** when you send.
**There’s less noise** next to what you’re typing.

content.alt: Three Newly prompt bars in Build, Plan and Ask mode, with only the active mode labelled
content.caption: Build, Plan and Ask. Only the active mode carries a label.

content.alt: The Newly prompt bar in expanded, stacked and collapsed layouts
content.caption: Expanded, stacked, collapsed.

content: A session can’t switch between remote and local once it starts. Only the model can change, and people rarely change it. So in a new session, location and model sit under the bar where you can’t miss them. Mid-chat, the model moves into the + menu, out of the way, especially for non-technical people.
These menus had to give clear information without much text. Each option gets a name and, at most, one short line:

bullets: **Location** explains its trade-off: “Runs in the cloud, accessible on any device” or “Runs on your computer, device must stay awake”.

**Models** say what you’re picking: Newly Agent is “Best all around”, and Codex and Claude “Use your own subscription”. If you haven’t linked one yet, a small **+ LINK** next to it prompts you to link your own.
**Effort** is a slider with one word for the current level, like “Medium”.

content.alt: Three popovers from the Newly prompt bar: Remote or Local session, Effort and Model, and the + menu with the model submenu
content.caption: The location and model menus at the start, and the + menu mid-chat.

bullets: A **stop** button while it runs.
A **status line** while it connects or fixes a bug.

A **queue**, so you don’t lose your next thought. Runs can take minutes, and people wanted to line up their next change instead of waiting. Queued messages sit above the bar, where you can see and remove them.

content.alt: Eight states of the Newly prompt bar: drop files, attached images, audio message, stop, connecting, fixing bugs, and messages in queue
content.caption: Drop files, images, voice, stop, connecting, fixing bugs and the queue.

sections.title: Conversation
sections.heading: Showing the agent’s work
content: The agent’s work folds into one line, like “Worked for 3m, used 3 tools”.

bullets: **Not everyone needs the commands.** Newly is for non-technical people too.
**The chat stays readable** instead of turning into a log.
**It’s still there to check.** Expanded, each step gets an icon, and code and commands sit in their own containers.

content.alt: The Newly chat panel on the blue wallpaper: the user’s message, the agent’s reply with its work folded into Worked for 3m, used 3 tools, and the prompt bar at the bottom
content.caption: The agent’s work, folded into one line, with the prompt bar below.

content: I used Claude Design to prototype the chat’s interactions and layouts. I could actually type and chat with the agent while I iterated on the designs.

bullets: **Markdown** in replies: headings, lists, inline code, tables and links.
**Code and terminal** blocks: a live terminal, code with its filename, and diffs.
**The tool list, expanded:** each tool with an icon and how long it took, and steps still running.
**Questions in the chat bar:** when the agent needs an answer, the bar turns into options to pick from.

content.alt: Four Newly chat experiments as selected frames on a dot grid: markdown in a reply, code and terminal blocks, the expanded tool list, and a question in the chat bar
content.caption: Four chat experiments from Claude Design.

sections.title: Simulator picker
sections.heading: A clearer simulator picker
content: The preview runs your app on an iPhone simulator, in the cloud or on your computer. The simulator picker went through eight versions.
Tester feedback and my own critique pointed to two problems:

bullets: **Unclear what was selected →** Cloud and Local got their own column, and the columns got labels: Type, Device, Version.
**Unclear what Apply did →** it re-runs the app, so Apply became Apply & Run.

content.alt: Four versions of the iOS simulator picker, from a footer Cloud/Local toggle and an Apply button to labelled Type, Device and Version columns with Apply & Run
content.caption: Four of the eight versions.

sections.title: Also shipped
sections.heading: Deploy, web and colour
content: I designed and built the deploy and web screens, and both are live.

bullets: **Deploy** groups destinations by platform. The App Store card shows a short checklist and the details already filled in.
**The web app** opens with a “Pick up where you left off” card to reopen your last project.
**Colour** is held back in the workspace. Blue only marks the active mode, the main action and anything running, so your own app stands out.

gallery.alt: The Newly Deploy hub with iOS, Android and Web destinations
The App Store release card with a checklist and an Automatically Completed list
Newly on the web: the welcome screen with a filled prompt and a Pick up where you left off card

content.caption: The Deploy hub, the App Store release card and the web welcome screen.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: What shipped and what I learned
content: The workspace, the prompt bar and its states, the deploy flow and the web app are all live.

bullets: **Shaped by feedback:** chat over the board, one sidebar instead of two, and Apply & Run in the simulator picker.
**After shipping:** people stopped getting stuck on the simulator picker.
Designing for an agent is mostly states, not screens.
A good idea can still be wrong for the timeline. The board may come back.

content: One prompt in Newly drives sessions, a simulator, models and App Store releases, for technical and non-technical people. As the only designer, I designed the workspace around that prompt bar. I also built the layout, the prompt bar, and the deploy and web screens in React and TypeScript. I prototyped the chat and the onboarding in Claude Design.
Feedback and the team’s priorities changed the plan more than once along the way. What shipped helped grow Newly’s revenue.
